title: Man. Post. Cap. II: Placeus ὀράματα 3–4 — mediate reasons; peace fails if precise immediate remains; before §III
pass_a_gloss: Then, he not only loses labor in proving against me that which I everywhere affirm, but, what is worse, he tries to elicit it from there, where it does not lie hidden. For although my words at first sight seem to favor his inference, yet every handle is cut off from him by the explanation which continuously follows, which he himself had thus contracted at page 33 of his book, because, as truly as Adam's sin passes into us, so truly it is said to be imputed to us. But it passes and has been propagated, not as it was a transient act, but as it was a permanent viciousness, nor as it was the sin of a person, but as it was the sin of nature, which namely adheres to human nature, and with it is multiplied and propagated. Third, it is false that all our reasons, if they effect anything, effect that we are in no way guilty on account of Adam's disobedience: For that they in no way impugn the mediate imputation of that disobedience I showed so clearly by letters given to him, that I could obtain a response from him by no agitation. Fourth finally it is false what he says, that if it remains fixed that Adam's act taken together with the corruption which it brought forth is imputed to each of the posterity, peace will easily be composed. For the entire question will remain, whether that act taken precisely is imputed immediately, that is, so that the corruption of that imputed act is a penalty properly so called. Which alone I have constantly denied, and wished denied. For it must be imputed precise from the corruption which stuck in Adam and in us, if indeed corruption follows that imputation as penalty.
pass_b_english: Next, he not only wastes labor proving against me what I everywhere affirm, but—worse—tries to draw it from a place where it is not hidden. My words may at first glance seem to favor his inference; yet the explanation that follows at once cuts off every handle, the explanation he himself had shortened at page 33 of his book: because, as truly as Adam's sin passes into us, so truly it is said to be imputed to us. But it passes and has been propagated not as a passing act but as lasting viciousness; not as a person's sin but as nature's sin—what clings to human nature and is multiplied and propagated with it. Third, it is false that all our reasons, if they prove anything, prove that we are in no way guilty for Adam's disobedience: for that they do not touch the mediate imputation of that disobedience I showed so clearly in letters to him that I could get no answer from him by any urging. Fourth, and last, it is false that if Adam's act, taken with the corruption it produced, remains imputed to each of the posterity, peace will be easily made. The whole question will still stand: whether that act, taken precisely, is imputed immediately—that is, so that the corruption of the imputed act is a penalty in the proper sense. That alone I have constantly denied, and wished denied. For the act must be imputed cut off from the corruption that clung in Adam and in us, if corruption is to follow that imputation as its penalty.
source_text: Deinde, non modo perdit operam in eo contra me probando quod passim affirmo, sed, quod deterius est, id inde elicere conatur, ubi non latet. Etsi enim verba mea prima fronte favere videantur ejus collectioni, tamen ei praescindit omnem ansam, quae continuo sequitur explicatio, quam ipse libri sui pag. 33. sic contraxerat, quia, quam vere peccatum Adami in nos transit, tam vere nobis imputari dicitur. Atqui transit et propagatum est, non qua fuit actio transiens, sed qua fuit vitiositas permanens, nec qua fuit peccatum personae, sed qua fuit peccatum naturae, quod scilicet naturae humanae adhaeret, et cum ea multiplicatur atque propagatur. Tertio, falsum est nostras omnes rationes, si quid efficiunt, efficere nos nullo modo esse reos propter inobedientiam Adami: Eas enim imputationem illius inobedientiae mediatam nullo modo impugnare tam clare ostendi datis ad eum literis, ut ab eo responsionem nulla etiam agitatione impetrare potuerim. Quarto denique falsum est id quod ait, si fixum maneat actionem Adami simul cum corruptione quam peperit acceptam unicuique posterorum imputari, pacem facile compositum iri. Restabit enim integra quaestio, utrum illa actio praecise sumpta immediate imputetur, hoc est, ita, ut illius imputatae corruptio sit poena proprie dicta. Id quod unum duntaxat et constanter negavi, et negatum volui. Praecisam enim a corruptione, quae in Adamo et nobis haesit, imputari oportet, si quidem illam imputationem corruptio sequitur ut poena.
